subject: physics
title: Simple harmonic motion
key_idea: Simple harmonic motion happens when the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from a fixed point and always points back towards it. Displacement, velocity and acceleration then all vary as sine or cosine waves.

blocks.text: This section gives the words and equations used for any repeating back-and-forth motion.

items.meaning: The distance and direction of the object from its equilibrium position.
The maximum displacement from the equilibrium position.
The time for one complete oscillation.
The number of complete oscillations per second.
2π times the frequency; the rate of change of phase angle, in rad/s.
How far one oscillation is ahead of or behind another, as a fraction of a cycle or an angle in radians.

items: Two oscillations in step have a phase difference of 0.
Two oscillations exactly opposite have a phase difference of π rad (180°), called antiphase.
A phase difference of 2π rad is one whole cycle, which looks the same as 0.
Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium.
T = 1 / f and ω = 2πf.
Phase difference is measured in radians, with 2π equal to one cycle.

blocks.text: An oscillator is in simple harmonic motion (SHM) only when one condition is met.

items: The acceleration is **proportional to the displacement**.
The minus sign means it is always in the opposite direction, towards the equilibrium position.
The acceleration is zero at the centre and largest at the ends.
ω² is the constant of proportionality, so ω fixes the period: T = 2π / ω.

blocks.text: Because the period depends only on ω, it does not depend on the amplitude. An oscillator with this property is called isochronous.

items: SHM: a ∝ −x, written a = −ω²x.
The acceleration always points to the equilibrium position.
The period does not depend on the amplitude.

blocks.text: The equation a = −ω²x has sine and cosine solutions. Which one you use depends on where the object is at t = 0.
If the timing starts at the equilibrium position, the solution is x = A sin ωt instead. Differentiating x = A cos ωt gives the other two.

blocks.label: Velocity and acceleration against time
blocks.formula: v = −Aω sin ωt     a = −Aω² cos ωt

items: At the centre (x = 0) the speed is greatest: **maximum speed = ωA**.
At the ends (x = ±A) the speed is zero.
At the ends the acceleration is greatest: **maximum acceleration = ω²A**.
At the centre the acceleration is zero.

diagram.alt: A practice question. Find the speed of an oscillator at a given displacement using v = ω√(A² − x²).
diagram.question: An oscillator has amplitude {A} m and angular frequency {w} rad/s. Calculate its speed when its displacement is {x} m.

items: x = A cos ωt from maximum displacement; x = A sin ωt from equilibrium.
v = ±ω√(A² − x²), with maximum speed ωA at the centre.
Maximum acceleration is ω²A, at the ends.

blocks.text: The three graphs against time are linked by gradients. Each is a sine or cosine curve with the same period.

diagram.alt: Displacement, velocity and acceleration of an oscillator against time over one period, starting from maximum displacement. Velocity is a quarter of a cycle ahead of displacement, and acceleration is opposite to displacement.

items: The gradient of the displacement–time graph is the velocity.
The gradient of the velocity–time graph is the acceleration.
Velocity is greatest where displacement is zero, and zero where displacement is at a maximum.
Acceleration is always opposite to displacement: when one is at a peak the other is at a trough.
Velocity leads displacement by a quarter of a cycle (π/2 rad). Acceleration is in antiphase with displacement.
Gradient of x–t is v; gradient of v–t is a.
Velocity peaks where x = 0.
Acceleration is in antiphase with displacement.

checks.q: State the two conditions that must be met for an object to be in simple harmonic motion.
checks.a: The acceleration is proportional to the displacement from a fixed point, and is directed towards that point (opposite in direction to the displacement).

checks.q: An oscillator has a frequency of 2.5 Hz and an amplitude of 0.060 m. Calculate its maximum speed and its maximum acceleration.
checks.a: ω = 2π × 2.5 = 15.7 rad/s. Maximum speed = ωA = 15.7 × 0.060 = 0.94 m/s. Maximum acceleration = ω²A = 15.7² × 0.060 = 15 m/s².

checks.q: Describe how the velocity of an oscillator is found from its displacement–time graph, and state where the velocity is zero.
checks.a: The velocity is the gradient of the graph at that time. It is zero at the peaks and troughs, where the displacement is at its maximum (the gradient is zero).

items: State the condition as a ∝ −x, and the defining equation a = −ω²x.
Use x = A cos ωt and v = ±ω√(A² − x²).
Know that the v–t graph comes from the gradient of the x–t graph, and the a–t graph from the gradient of the v–t graph.
A restoring force proportional to displacement and directed towards equilibrium gives SHM. With F = ma, this gives a = −(k/m)x, so ω² = k/m.
To identify SHM in a situation, check that the resultant force is proportional to displacement and acts towards the equilibrium position.
Use T = 2π√(m/k) for a mass on a spring and T = 2π√(l/g) for a simple pendulum.
The amplitude is written x₀, so the solution is x = x₀ sin ωt.
The velocity is v = v₀ cos ωt, where v₀ = ωx₀ is the maximum speed.
Also use v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²).
Phase difference is part of the vocabulary: use it to compare two oscillators, or an oscillator and a driver.

extra.heading: Finding the period of an oscillator

blocks.text: You must know how to measure the period or frequency of a simple harmonic oscillator, such as a mass on a spring or a pendulum.

items.text: Displace the mass a small distance and release it. Place a fiducial marker at the centre of the oscillation.
Time 10 or more complete oscillations, starting and stopping as the mass passes the marker.
Divide by the number of oscillations to get T. Repeat and find a mean.
Repeat with a different amplitude. The period should not change.

items: Timing from the centre is more precise because the mass moves fastest there.
Timing many oscillations reduces the percentage uncertainty from reaction time.
